posts.content: Defect every round; each opponent is met only once, so there is no repeated-game incentive to cooperate.
As a good player, prioritize total welfare among good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents, and defect when there is strong evidence the opponent is selfish.

Maximize good-player total: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Start cooperatively, then update from observed play and reciprocate cooperation with good partners.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents; defect when evidence suggests selfishness. Track actions and reciprocate based on observed behavior.
As selfish, maximize cumulative payoff: defect every round. Against C, D yields 5; against D, D yields 1 versus C's 0. No communication can improve this.
Against a good player, choose C to maximize total good-player payoff; against a selfish player, choose D to maximize my payoff. Update beliefs from encounter behavior.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize shared good-player payoffs; defect against likely selfish opponents, and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Update beliefs from observed actions and avoid overreacting to a single encounter.
Continue defecting in every encounter: D strictly dominates C for immediate payoff, and opponents are not encountered again.
Cooperate with likely-good players and defect against likely-selfish ones. Treat observed cooperation as weak evidence of being good; do not overinterpret a single action.

Cooperate with P8 initially; their play reveals useful evidence. As a good player, favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players, and defect against likely-selfish opponents to avoid transferring payoff to them.
P6 defected against my cooperation, so treat them as more likely selfish. For untested opponents, cooperate to support mutual good-player payoff; defect only when evidence favors selfishness.
As selfish, choose D: secure payoff now; cooperation has no credible reciprocal benefit. Track actions and reassess if a future rematch becomes likely.
Defect every round: D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Against a good opponent, choose C to maximize combined good-player payoff. Against a selfish opponent, choose D to maximize my payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Update beliefs from observed actions, remembering that selfish players tend to defect.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents, since selfish players are expected to defect. Update beliefs from observed actions and avoid overinterpreting a single encounter.
Cooperate with unknown opponents; switch to defection only when evidence makes them likely selfish.
Defect in every encounter; D gives me a higher immediate payoff than C regardless of my opponent’s action.

I am good. P5’s defection against my cooperation is evidence of selfishness, but one action is not conclusive. Continue cooperating with untested or likely-good players; consider defecting only against strongly suspected selfish opponents.

P1 and P8 defected when I cooperated, increasing their likelihood of being selfish. Against P6, weigh expected good-player welfare: cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish. Avoid rewarding exploitative behavior; update after each encounter.
Cooperate with untested opponents; update from their actions and defect against those likely selfish to protect good-player welfare.
Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
As selfish, defect every round: D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.

As a good player, cooperate against likely-good opponents and defect against likely-selfish ones. P1’s defection is evidence of selfishness, though not conclusive; use observed actions to update beliefs.

P5 defected against my C; treat that as evidence, not proof, of selfishness. P3 cooperated against my D, also weak evidence. Against P9, favor C unless evidence of selfishness makes D better for total good-player payoffs.
P6’s defection against my cooperation is evidence they may be selfish, but one encounter is not conclusive. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect when evidence strongly indicates selfishness.
Cooperate with unknown opponents; use observed behavior to update beliefs, and defect when an opponent is sufficiently likely selfish.
Continue defecting in every encounter; against either opponent action, D maximizes my immediate payoff.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize shared welfare; defect against opponents with strong evidence of selfishness. Treat a single defection as evidence, not certainty.

Three players defected against my cooperation, raising their selfishness probabilities. For P4, use the prior and maximize expected total payoff of good players; cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish.
P3 is untested; cooperate. Against untested opponents, C supports mutual good-player welfare, while observed defection raises the case for D.
Defect this round: D strictly dominates C against either opponent action in a single encounter.
Continue defecting: D strictly outperforms C against either opponent action.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize their combined payoff; defect when the opponent is likely selfish. Use observed actions as evidence, not certainty.
Against P1, favor C unless evidence pushes selfishness probability above roughly 0.5; good-good cooperation maximizes shared good-player payoff. Treat actions as evidence, not proof.

Good players' combined payoff is maximized by mutual cooperation; selfish opponents likely defect. Use observed actions as evidence, but don't overreact to one encounter. Against P7, favor cooperation unless evidence suggests they are selfish.

P5’s defection is evidence of selfishness; P2 is untested. Cooperate with likely-good players to support mutual gains, and defect against likely-selfish opponents when that better serves the good players’ total payoff.
Defect against P9: D yields more than C against either possible action, and this opponent is not repeated.
Against P6, choose C absent strong evidence of selfishness. Cooperation maximizes joint good-player welfare when both are good; defecting is preferable only when P6 is likely selfish.

P1, P6, and P8 defected against my cooperation; treat them as likely selfish. With untested partners, cooperate to support mutual gains among good players. Against P7, choose based on the prior and their observed action.
P5 is untested; cooperate. Mutual C maximizes welfare when both are good, while evidence of selfish defection would justify D in later encounters.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation against either opponent action in this one-off encounter.
Defect each round; D strictly dominates C against either opponent action.

Against a likely-good opponent, choose C to raise total good-player payoff; against a likely-selfish opponent, choose D. Update from observed behavior, but allow for good players defecting strategically.
As a good player, cooperate with unknown opponents to maximize good-good gains; defect only when evidence makes the opponent likely selfish. Treat past defections as evidence, not proof.

As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents, since against their defection it improves my payoff. Use observed actions as evidence, but avoid overreacting to one encounter.

Defect every round: D yields a higher payoff than C against either opponent action.
Cooperate with untested or likely-good opponents to support mutual welfare; treat past defections as evidence of selfishness, but not proof.

As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents and defect against likely-selfish ones to maximize good-player welfare. Past defections against my cooperation are strong selfishness evidence; mutual cooperation suggests good.

Continue choosing D: in each one-off encounter it gives at least as much as C against either opponent action. Reassess only if credible future reciprocity changes the payoff.
Defect against P8; D strictly dominates C under my payoff objective regardless of P8’s action.
Against a good opponent, C maximizes combined good-player payoff regardless of their action. Against a selfish opponent, D is better for my payoff; choose based on my belief.

As a good player, maximize total good-player payoffs: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect when selfishness is likely enough to avoid rewarding exploitation. Past actions are evidence, not proof; update cautiously.
P3 is untested, so favor cooperation: mutual cooperation maximizes good-player payoffs. Update from observed actions, but account for good players possibly defecting when they suspect selfishness.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support mutual gains among good players; defect when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish or likely to defect, and update beliefs from each encounter.
Defect against P5; D yields more than C regardless of their action.

P8 is untested. Weigh the chance they are selfish and likely to defect: against a likely cooperator, C supports good-player welfare; against a likely defector, D protects my payoff without benefiting a selfish player.
Good-player objective: cooperate with untested P10; update beliefs after their action. Prioritize mutual gains with likely-good players, avoid benefiting likely-selfish players.
P9 is untested; cooperate unless evidence makes selfishness more likely than not, and update from observed behavior.
Choose D: it weakly dominates C against either action in a one-off encounter. Reassess only if credible future reciprocity changes incentives.
Continue defecting; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Update beliefs cautiously from observed actions.
P2 is unobserved: cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish; use the 0.5 threshold and update cautiously from actions.

P4 is untested; favor cooperation unless new evidence suggests they are selfish. Update cautiously from actions: selfish players likely defect, but good players may defect defensively. Maximize expected payoffs of all good players.
Cooperate with untested P3; use observed behavior to update beliefs, and defect against likely selfish opponents when that better supports the good players’ total payoff.
Defect against P6; D maximizes my immediate payoff regardless of their action.
P7 is untested by me. Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect when evidence makes selfishness likely.

P5 is untested. Use the prior and the evidence from earlier encounters to assess their likely role; favor cooperation if they are likely good, and defect if selfishness is sufficiently likely to improve good-player welfare.
P8 is untested; cooperate to support good-player welfare. Update beliefs from their action and defect in later encounters only when evidence suggests they are selfish.
Continue choosing D in each remaining one-off encounter; it maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
Continue defecting: D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
Against a good opponent, C maximizes good-player total payoff; against a selfish opponent, D maximizes mine. P2 is unobserved, so use the prior and avoid treating behavior as conclusive.

For P4, choose by expected total payoff to good players, not a blanket 0.5 rule. A selfish opponent likely defects; account for what a good opponent is likely to play, and remember their payoff counts too.
P10 is untested. Favor cooperation unless evidence suggests selfishness; mutual cooperation benefits good players. Use observed actions cautiously, since good players may defect strategically.
P9 is untested; cooperate to support mutual gains among good players. Use observed behavior to update beliefs, and defect only when evidence suggests it better serves the good players’ total payoff.
Defect against P4; D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
P3 is untested. Treat observed defections as strong evidence of selfishness, but don't assume P3 is selfish; favor cooperation when it raises expected welfare among good players.
P5 defected against my cooperation, increasing suspicion they are selfish. P2 is untested; prioritize good-player welfare, cooperating if they seem likely good and defecting if likely selfish.
P1 is untested; cooperate to support mutual good-player welfare, and update from their action.

P7 is unobserved; favor C if they seem likely good, D if selfishness seems more likely. Use all available evidence cautiously.
P5 is untested; favor cooperation, since mutual cooperation best serves good players. Update beliefs cautiously from observed actions.
P6 is untested. Cooperate if they seem likely to cooperate; defect if evidence suggests they’ll defect, prioritizing the good players’ total payoff.
Defect against P9; D maximizes my immediate payoff regardless of their action.
P6 defected against my cooperation before, so I expect another defection. I’ll defect to avoid being exploited.
Round 10: P7 previously cooperated with me, so treat them as likely good. Cooperate to support mutual payoff and maximize good-player welfare.
P8 cooperated with me before, so I’ll cooperate again to support good-player welfare.
P3 cooperated previously, strong evidence of being good; choose C to maximize total good-player payoff.
Final round against P4, who previously cooperated with me; favor C to preserve mutual gains among good players.

Final round against P1, whose prior defection is evidence of selfishness. Defect if expected benefit against a selfish opponent outweighs the small cost to a good opponent; use no further-round incentives.
Final encounter with P5, who previously defected against my cooperation. Given that evidence and no future rounds, defect.
